schools.summary: Ellicott: each friend has now supplied his quota, and Job answers the third, showing himself far more conversant with the wisdom and majesty of God than they, though they alone in their own esteem are wise.
Gill reads the formula as a reply to Zophar and a defence of himself, the substance filling this and the next two chapters.
Henry hears a rebuke to the proud and scornful, yet weighs whether the reproof was just — the friends meant to convince, and we are apt to call reproofs reproaches.
Clarke lays out the chapter's argument: Job reproves the friends' boasting, asserts even robbers' tents prosper, yet God governs the world as all creation proclaims.

themes: the reply as argument not outburst
God the Governor of the world

schools.summary: Gill hears biting irony — Job ridicules the friends' self-conceit as if they were 'the people,' the only wise men, all others fools and asses (an echo of Zophar's wild ass's colt).

Clarke calls it 'a strong irony'; Wesley reads it the same, yet draws the comfort that wisdom does not die with the wise, since God keeps the fulness of the Spirit in his own hand and can raise up others.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh 'truly then ye are the people' (the whole race of men, as Isa. 40:7), note the LXX's 'are ye alone men?', and reject Ewald's modern rendering 'I also have a head' — the Hebrew says heart.

outliers.note: Rejects Ewald's rendering 'I also have a head even as you' as a western, modern, unbiblical expression; the Hebrew word is heart, the seat of understanding.

themes: wisdom does not die with the wise

schools.summary: Gill takes 'understanding' as natural (parting man from brute) and spiritual (knowing God and his living Redeemer), and fills out the variant 'I have a heart as well as you' — as upright and sincere as theirs.

Clarke: Job falls short of none of them, and their wisdom is but 'strings of proverbs in every person's mouth'; Wesley guards it as vindication, not boasting, of himself and God's cause (Job 42:7), since even barbarous nations know God is infinite — 'but this is not the question between you and me.'
Gill reports Sephorno's turn but prefers that Job instances himself as proof the godly are afflicted — once caressed, now the scorn of his neighbours, mocked by the friends who came to comfort him.

Clarke: 'though I invoke God, my friends mock me — but God answereth me,' owning the verse very difficult ('to emendations there is no end'); Wesley: the mockers are religious neighbours who call on God, yet Job dares own that by grace he is upright.
Ellicott frames it as either Job's own character or the friends' supposed taunt — the righteous and perfect a laughing-stock — with the maxim 'ridicule is no test of truth or of merit.'

debates.question: Is 'the just upright man is laughed to scorn' Job's claim about himself or the friends' taunt?

sides.position: Job claims the character for himself — the praying, upright man mocked
it may be the supposed taunt of the friends; either way, ridicule proves nothing

themes: the standing lot of the upright

schools.summary: Ellicott owns the received words 'convey no sense' and offers two renderings — the torch for tottering feet rejected by the man at ease, or, more probably, contempt for calamity lying ready in the easy man's thoughts.
Gill reads the slipping as into calamity, not sin, and takes Job as the man 'ready to slip,' made the laughing-stock of the secure and unstable.
Wesley: though he once shone as a lamp, the fallen man is now the snuff of a candle thrown down and trodden, despised in the thought of him at ease.
Henry names the sin on the other side — the prosperous scorn the afflicted; poverty eclipses a man's lustre, lamps moved from golden candlesticks into earthen pitchers.

debates.question: How is 'a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease' to be rendered?

sides.position: the torch prepared for tottering feet, disregarded by those at ease who need no aid
contempt for calamity is what lies ready in the thoughts of the man at ease

schools.summary: Gill points the robbers at the Chaldeans and Sabeans who plundered Job and prosper still — a fact that has tempted good men in every age to question God's justice.

Henry sets the verse against Zophar (11:20): God acts as sovereign, reserving exact reward and punishment for the future state; even robbers' tents prosper, so 'we cannot judge of men's piety by their plenty.'
Clarke: prosperity and adversity are no evidence of a man's spiritual state; Wesley: the friends supposed the wicked cannot prosper long, but God reserves the exact reckoning for the other world.
Ellicott notes the alternative rendering 'to him that bringeth his god in his hand' (cf. Hab. 1:11) but prefers the common construction of 'into whose hand God bringeth abundantly.'

debates.question: How is the last clause of v.6 to be rendered?

sides.position: 'into whose hand God bringeth abundantly' — God's providence supplies even the wicked
'to him that bringeth his god in his hand' (cf. Hab. 1:11), whose might is his god

themes: reward reserved for the future state

schools.summary: Gill draws from the creatures the very lesson the friends deny — the harmless fall prey to the strong (lambs to lions, lesser fish to greater), and the flocks serve wicked men more than good.

Wesley: what Zophar uttered so pompously (11:7) needs no journey to heaven or hell — 'thou mayst learn it even from the beasts'; Clarke, via Good, has Job say all nature owns God as Creator, but to apply it as a charge of hypocrisy is impertinent, and why good and evil are scattered the friends are 'as ignorant of as myself.'
Henry hears the creatures teach both that robbers prosper (the greater devour the less, Hab. 1:14) and that God's wisdom and dominion, Zophar's great mystery, lie open in the book of the creatures.

themes: the friends made pupils of the creatures

schools.summary: Gill bids one ask 'a sprig of the earth,' any shrub or tree, which unites in the doctrine that all are raised and preserved by God's power — instances of his wisdom, power, and goodness.

Keil and Delitzsch, taking the strophe down through v.11, correct the reading that makes the creatures teach Job's hard destiny: they teach rather that the hand of the LORD has wrought all this and holds the soul of every living thing.

debates.question: What do the earth and the creatures teach?

sides.position: that all things are raised and preserved by God's power — his wisdom, power, and goodness
not the lesson of Job's undeserved suffering, but the universal dominion of God's hand over all living things

themes: all creation held in God's hand

schools.summary: Gill: what man is so senseless he cannot learn from the creatures what Zophar discoursed of, since by the things made the invisible things of God are clearly seen (Rom. 1:20)?

Ellicott: this is the only place in the dialogue where the name Jehovah appears, and Job's use of the covenant name is the clearest evidence of the superior knowledge he claims — no friend ever uses it.
Wesley confirms it is the only time the name Jehovah occurs in the discourses, God in that age being more known as Shaddai, the Almighty.

outliers.note: Marks that 'Jehovah' occurs only here in the whole dialogue of Job, and reads Job's use of the covenant name as proof of a knowledge of God superior to that of his friends, who never use it.

schools.summary: Gill: the life of every animal is from God, continued at his pleasure and not taken without his leave — not a sparrow falls without his will (Matt. 10:29).
Clarke presses the two phrases — 'the soul of all life' and 'the breath of all flesh' — asking whether the first points to the immortal soul and the second to respiration (cf. Job 10:1).
Henry resolves all into God's absolute propriety: all creatures derive their being from him and lie at his disposal — 'all souls are his; and may he not do what he will with his own?'

themes: the soul of every living thing

schools.summary: Gill: the ear tries articulate sounds and the mind judges true from false, as spiritual ears discern the wholesome words of Christ from false teachers, bringing all to the standard of the sanctuary.
Clarke turns it on the friends: 'all these are common-place sayings; ye have advanced nothing new, cast no light upon the dispensations of Providence.'

Ellicott: the wise man must discriminate, not accept all he receives, and the true Ancient of Days is wise indeed; Keil and Delitzsch fix the waw of likeness — the ancients' sayings must be proved, the ear testing them as the palate tastes food (cf. Heb. 5:14).
Henry: the mind discerns truth from error as the palate sweet from bitter; Job demands liberty to judge what the friends said and appeals to any impartial hearing to try the words on both sides.

themes: sifting tradition, not bowing to it
Job's claim to a fair hearing

schools.summary: Gill turns over the proverb — Job wishing an aged man to arbitrate, or answering Bildad's counsel to search the fathers, allowing wisdom is with them only as far as it agrees with God's — best taken as the general truth that long years gather wisdom.
Keil and Delitzsch let the concession to grey heads stand only to be surpassed at once: with God are wisdom and strength together, and all opposed to him is powerless.

Henry contrasts human and divine wisdom — the aged get it slowly and then lack strength to execute it, but with God are both wisdom and strength: 'what is the wisdom of ancient men compared with the wisdom of the Ancient of days?'

Gill refers the words to God, not the aged man: wisdom dwells with him originally, essentially, and underived, displayed in creation, providence, and redemption — so the Gospel is called the wisdom of God.
Clarke: all these come from God, the Fountain of wisdom and Source of power, who alone gives unerring counsel and understanding to act by it.

Henry knits the four terms into one perfection — with men wisdom and strength are parted, but with God are both, had essentially and eternally, so the happy have this God for their God and men's attempts against him are fruitless.

themes: with him is wisdom and strength

schools.summary: Gill runs through the ruins never rebuilt — Sodom, Thebes, Tyre, the kingdoms Jeremiah rooted out, the four monarchies broken by the kingdom of Christ.

Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as proof God is almighty and all opposed to him powerless — a sealed dungeon (cf. Lam. 3:53) that cannot be opened; Ellicott: 'God has equal power over the moral and physical world.'

Clarke: God alone can create and destroy; not a particle can be annihilated but by him — Nineveh, Babylon, Tyre, the great empires broken past recovery; Wesley carries 'no opening' to the grave and hell, whose sealed doors none can force.

themes: power over moral and physical world

schools.summary: Gill reads the withholding of the waters of God restraining the sea at creation, drawing off the flood, or binding the rain in the clouds till the brooks fail (as Cherith).

Clarke fixes the two allusions — the third day's gathering of the waters (Gen. 1:9) and the breaking up of the great deep at the flood; Wesley reads the same, the waters reserved in the clouds withheld, then the deluge loosed to overturn the earth.
Keil and Delitzsch set the verse in the strophe as proof God disposes the elements at will, bringing drought or flood upon a land.

Henry: God binds the waters as in a garment (Prov. 30:4) and holds them in his hand (Isa. 40:12), punishing by defect (drought) or excess (flood) — many ways of contending with a sinful people none can withstand.
Gill takes the first clause as a repetition of v.13, ascribing to God the greatest might and most substantial wisdom.

Clarke finds the repetition only apparent — v.13 was wisdom guiding power, here strength in essence, self-existent and self-sufficient — and asks whether 'the deceived and the deceiver' reach back to the fall (Satan, Adam and Eve; cf. Heb. 2:11); Wesley: God governs the deceiver and sets bounds to his deceits, yet is not the author of sin, only its wise and holy governor.
Henry: God makes use even of the foolish and the bad — the simplest dupe and the subtlest cheat are his, Jacob's fraud serving grace and Ahab's false prophecy serving justice (Ezek. 14:9).

debates.question: What is meant by 'the deceived and the deceiver are his'?

sides.position: it reaches back to the fall — Satan the deceiver, Adam and Eve the deceived, all claimed by God
God's overruling of every deceit and dupe in the world, serving grace and justice, though not authoring sin

outliers.note: Reads 'the deceived and the deceiver are his' as possibly reaching back to the fall — Satan the deceiver and Adam and Eve the deceived, both God's, the seed of the woman appointed to bruise the serpent (Heb. 2:11).

themes: God governs deceit he never authors

schools.summary: Gill: God spoils the ablest counsellors of their wisdom, confounds their schemes, and carries their counsel headlong, stripping them of both the fame and the fruit of their sagacity.
Keil and Delitzsch dispute the word 'spoiled' — not chained (Targum) nor made booty (LXX) but 'stripped of their robes,' divested of the insignia of office.

Clarke reads the events of war — counsellors led captive and found among the spoils, judges infatuated; Wesley: statesmen led away in triumph, spoiled of wisdom or dignity, and judges made fools by God turning their counsels to their ruin.

Henry: God leads counsellors away as trophies while his own counsel stands, and makes judges fools — Ahithophel's counsel became folly, the princes of Zoan befooled (Isa. 19:13); let no wise man glory in his wisdom.

themes: stripped of the robes of office

schools.summary: Gill weighs the bond — the yoke kings lay on subjects, which God loosens by freeing the oppressed, or the king's own waistband, ungirding and unkinging him, for God sets up and removes kings at pleasure.

Clarke reads dethronement — robes exchanged for sackcloth, authority dissolved, kings bound as captives; Wesley: God frees the subjects from the kings' power and then girds the kings' own loins into a servile condition, deposing them into slavery.

Ellicott construes it as loosing 'the confederacy of kings' and girding them to fight one another (or the girdle of servitude against the girdle of state); Keil and Delitzsch supply the vocabulary of the invincible and tested whom God strips, noting v.21 repeats Ps. 107:40 verbatim.
Henry: God unbuckles the belts of kings so the sword and then the crown drop, girding their loins with the badge of servitude — 'to us they are gods, but men to him.'

debates.question: What 'bond of kings' does God loose?

sides.position: the yoke of bondage kings lay on their subjects, or the king's own royal girdle of authority
the confederacy by which kings bind themselves together, then girded to fight each other

themes: he looseth the bond of kings

schools.summary: Gill allows both — princes stripped of dominion, or 'priests,' since no sacred office protects wicked men (LXX 'he leads the priests captives'), from whom the law perishes.
Clarke leans to priests spoiled of power and mighty men overthrown, noting how many priests of Israel and Judah were led away if the book was written after the captivity.

Ellicott settles for princes (the parallelism suits it), and reads the whole latter half as Job re-echoing Eliphaz (5:11-16) but turning it to blank despair — Job the type of one who feels the hollowness of traditional orthodoxy yet holds an unquenchable faith, declaring nations, not men only, the subjects of God's providence.

sides.position: priests — no sacred office protects wicked men (LXX)
princes — the parallelism suits it better

outliers.note: Reads the latter half of the chapter as Job re-echoing Eliphaz (5:11-16) but turning it from optimism to blank despair — Job the type of the man feeling his way in darkness, whose unquenchable faith is more acceptable to God than Eliphaz's confident key to providence.

themes: faith feeling its way in darkness

schools.summary: Gill grounds it in God's ownership of the tongue — his to give and take, at death, or by striking dumb (Zechariah), confounding speech (Babel), or letting a man say the contrary of his intent (Balaam).

Wesley: God removes utterance or the understanding that directs it, the 'trusty' being counsellors princes leaned on; Clarke: 'quos Deus vult perdere, prius dementat' — the eloquent and the elders avail nothing to save a state God means to destroy (cf. Isa. 3:1).
Keil and Delitzsch carry the strophe on toward the deep things brought to light.

Henry: the eloquent are silenced or made to speak the contrary of their purpose (Balaam blessing whom he would curse), and the aged deprived of wisdom by the infirmities that make them twice children — 'an old and foolish king' (Eccl. 4:13).

themes: 'whom God would destroy he first infatuates'

schools.summary: Gill limits the contempt to bad princes — tyrants and persecutors (Herod, Pilate, the persecuting emperors, antichristian powers) whom God deposes, debases, or cuts off by shameful deaths.
Henry: God pours contempt on princes by leaving them to mean things or altering men's opinion of them — none more abject when down than the once haughty (Ps. 107:40).

Clarke reads 'the mighty' as the compact and sinewy (the crocodile's frame, Job 40:13) and 'weakeneth the strength' as 'looseth the girdle' — God alone can loose the girdles of that mighty one (Job 40:19).

themes: God takes down what men lift up

schools.summary: Gill lifts it to the deep things of God himself — the thoughts of his heart (Ps. 92:5), the deep things the Spirit reveals (1 Cor. 2:10), the decrees and the love hid till brought to light in Christ.

Clarke: God's works in the great deep, or the plots of the wicked hidden till death glut himself with carnage; Wesley: the most secret counsels of princes, contrived in the dark, dragged into open day.
Keil and Delitzsch: nothing is so finely spun that God cannot make it visible — all the secret plans and veiled sins of the wicked he brings before the tribunal of the world.
Henry: plots laid are exposed and the guilty punished — secret treasons (Eccl. 10:20), murders, whoredoms — for the cabinet-councils of princes lie open before God (2 Kings 6:11).

debates.question: What 'deep things out of darkness' does God discover?

sides.position: the deep things of God himself — his thoughts, decrees, and love, revealed by their accomplishment
the hidden plots, sins, and secret counsels of wicked men, dragged into the light

schools.summary: Gill instances the nations destroyed at the flood, the seven nations of Canaan cleared for Israel, the four monarchies, and the antichristian states yet to fall.

Wesley: what Job said of princes he applies to nations, increased or diminished as God pleases; Clarke, via Good, reads 'he letteth the nations grow licentious' — luxury ripening to ruin by a hardier foe — all pronounced God's judgment and mercy, for he putteth down one and raiseth up another.

Ellicott hears the key to history — nations marked by differences, the wisest failing (Ahithophel), because One works underneath for his own ends; Job holds a deeper, inscrutable depth calling for faith, which only seems fatalism because he handles one side and would state man's responsibility (clay in the potter's hand) with equal force; Keil and Delitzsch render 'he giveth prosperity to nations and then destroyeth them.'
Henry: kingdoms have their waxings and wanings, both from God, who enlarges their bounds then straitens them till the head becomes the tail (Ps. 107:38).

outliers.note: Reads the verse as the key to history and Job's God-sovereignty as concerning nations, not men only; grants it may seem to savour of fatalism, but only because Job handles one side of the problem and would state man's responsibility, clay in the potter's hand, with equal force.

schools.summary: Gill reads the 'chief of the people' as kings, princes, and generals dispirited of courage and conduct — Sephorno's Sihon and Og, but better the Israelites and leaders discomfited by Amalek soon after Egypt.

Clarke hears a plain allusion to Israel's history — leaders panic-struck, and the wandering recalling the wilderness years and Aaron's failure of courage over the golden calf; Houbigant would refer it to colony-leaders, but the allusion to Israel is too apt to doubt.
Henry: the bold and courageous strangely cowed when God takes away their heart, ready to flee at the shaking of a leaf (Ps. 66:5).

themes: the heart of leaders taken away
made to wander in a pathless waste

schools.summary: Gill reads them as blind men groping — the men of Sodom struck blind, the Egyptians in the darkness that might be felt — seeking light and finding none.

Clarke traces the words to Moses' curse of groping at noonday (Deut. 28:28) and the reeling sailors of Ps. 107:27, and closes with Good's reflection that all the machinery of government is in God's hands — 'human pomp is poverty, human wisdom folly, human strength weakness'; Wesley: revolutions of kingdoms are brought about by an overruling providence, but the Lord remaineth a king for ever.
